Environmental impact — barrels spilled per million tons moved every mile: truck 326, pipeline 269, rail 83. Here rail wins and the pipeline comes second. This is the panel students misremember: the pipeline is the best on fatalities but not on spill volume, because a pipeline leak is rare but large, whereas a rail spill is more frequent but small.

How long does it take — Bakken field in North Dakota to the Gulf Coast: pipeline 40 days, rail 5-7 days.

The apparent contradiction sits in the last panel: the mode that is cheapest and safest is by far the slowest. Oil creeps through a trunk line at a few kilometres per hour, so a transcontinental pipeline takes weeks while a unit train takes under a week. That matters commercially in two ways. The oil inside the line is working capital that is tied up and price-exposed for 40 days — the line fill is a real, financed inventory. And a trader who wants to react to a price move needs rail, not pipeline. So the ranking depends entirely on the criterion: pipeline for cost and safety, rail for speed and for spill volume, truck only for the last mile.

The slide's own caveat is worth repeating: these are "Grobe Anhaltswerte", rough reference values from a single US study, not numbers to be transferred to Europe without care.

prompt: According to the comparison slide the cost of moving one barrel of oil is about $20 by truck, $10-$15 by rail and about ___ by pipeline.
solution: $5 per barrel — roughly a quarter of the truck cost and a third to a half of the rail cost. The same ranking appears in the safety panel (1.7 fatalities per year for the pipeline against 2.4 for rail and 10.2 for the truck), but not in the spill panel, where rail is best with 83 barrels per million ton-miles against 269 for the pipeline and 326 for the truck, and not in the duration panel, where the pipeline needs 40 days against 5-7 days by rail. The slide labels all of these "Grobe Anhaltswerte", rough reference values.

prompt: Reproduce the comparison table of road, rail, river and pipeline. Go through the criteria and then explain the two rows that are most often misunderstood: "investment" and "return costs".
solution:
The table compares four modes across eight criteria.

Investment — road: low by unit, high overall; rail: moderate by unit, high overall; river: high by unit if sound cost-effectiveness is required (push boat); pipeline: very high and made over a short period.
Infrastructure costs — road: none (borne by the public); rail: mainly borne by the State; river: toll duties; pipeline: high, and borne entirely by the company.
Personnel costs — road: very high; rail: fairly high; river: high for self-propelled barges, low for push boats; pipeline: low (personnel high in skills but low in numbers).
Maintenance costs — road: very high; rail and river: high except when volumes justify collective installations and automation; pipeline: very low.
Return costs — road: empty return; rail: empty return; river: return in ballast; pipeline: nil.
Length of route — road: outward practically everywhere, but natural obstacles impose significant detours; rail: fairly dense, limited by natural obstacles; river: the most circuitous route, where it exists at all; pipeline: the most direct.
Climatic conditions during transit — road: very sensitive; rail: not very sensitive; river: sensitive; pipeline: not affected.
Flexibility of use — road: very high; rail: very limited; river: very limited; pipeline: nil.

Investment. "Low by unit, high overall" for the road is not a contradiction. One truck is cheap, but thousands of them are needed for the same throughput, so the total capital tied up is large. The pipeline is the opposite: a single asset, very expensive, and — this is the important half of the sentence — the money has to be spent over a short period, before one single barrel flows. That is the classic lumpy, irreversible, sunk investment of a network industry, and it is why a pipeline is only built against long-term capacity contracts.

Return costs. Every vehicle-based mode has to bring the empty vehicle back; the return trip earns nothing but costs fuel, time and personnel, and the barge does it "in ballast", i.e. carrying water for stability. The pipeline has no return cost at all, because nothing travels back. This is a genuine and often forgotten cost advantage — the counterpart of its "nil" flexibility of use: the pipe does one thing, in one direction, for its whole life.

prompt: In the comparison table of transportation means, which pair of entries belongs to the pipeline column?
options: Return costs: return in ballast; climatic conditions: sensitive
Length of route: the most direct; flexibility of use: nil
Infrastructure costs: mainly borne by State; flexibility of use: very limited
Investment: low by unit, high overall; personnel costs: very high
solution: The pipeline column reads "The most direct" for the length of route and "Nil" for the flexibility of use — two sides of the same property: the line runs exactly where it was built and nowhere else. Option 1 is the rail column, where the State carries the infrastructure. Option 2 is the river column: a barge returns in ballast, while road and rail have an empty return and the pipeline has no return cost at all. Option 4 is the road column. The pipeline's own entries elsewhere in the table are very high investment made over a short period, infrastructure costs borne entirely by the company, low personnel costs, very low maintenance and no sensitivity to climatic conditions during transit.

prompt: The chart shows US crude oil refinery receipts by mode from 1981 to 2016 in thousand barrels. Describe the shares and the one visible structural change, and explain what caused it.
solution:
Pipeline dominates the whole period by a wide margin: it is the largest band on the chart throughout and accounts for the great majority of all refinery receipts. Tanker is the second mode, barge a clear third, while rail (tank cars) and truck are almost invisible for most of the thirty-five years.

The one structural change is the appearance of a rail band from about 2010, growing from essentially nothing to a visible share by 2014 and falling back afterwards.

The cause is the tight-oil (shale) boom, above all in the Bakken of North Dakota. Production grew far faster than pipelines could be permitted and built — a pipeline needs years of right-of-way acquisition and approval, a rail loading rack needs months — so the incremental barrels moved by rail to the coastal refineries, which were also willing to pay a premium because they were configured for imported light crude. As soon as the new pipeline capacity came into service, and after the 2014 price fall removed the incentive, the rail volumes collapsed again.

The same period explains the tanker band shrinking: US crude imports fell as domestic production rose.

The general lesson is that the mode split is not a preference but the outcome of a capacity race. Rail is the swing mode that fills the gap during the construction time of a pipeline, at a higher unit cost — roughly $10-$15 per barrel against $5 by pipeline on slide 296 — and that difference is exactly the premium the market was prepared to pay while the bottleneck lasted.

prompt: The Keystone pipeline has a capacity of 590,000 bbl/day in Phases I and II, rising to ___ bbl/day with Phase III.
solution: 700,000 bbl/day. Keystone carries Canadian oil-sands crude from Alberta to the US Midwest and, with Phase III (the Gulf Coast extension), on to the Gulf Coast refineries, which are configured for heavy sour crude and therefore pay the best price for it. For scale: even the expanded 700,000 bbl/day is less than half of the 1,500,000 bbl/day that slide 294 gives as the upper magnitude of a pipeline, and replacing it by rail would require 3,500 tank cars a day at the slide's 200 bbl per car.

prompt: The Shipping slide notes that a VLCC is "often used as storage at a single location". Explain when and why a tanker is used as a floating store instead of sailing, and how this connects to the negative oil price of slide 282.
solution:
A tanker is a tank that happens to float. Whenever the market is in contango — the forward price for a later delivery exceeds the spot price by more than the cost of carrying the barrel — it pays to buy oil now, store it and sell it forward. That is exactly the storage arbitrage condition of the gas chapter, p_supply + p_storage < p_sales, applied to oil: the spread has to beat the storage cost, and here the storage cost is the charter rate plus financing and insurance.

When the onshore tank farms are full or their fees rise, the marginal storage unit is a chartered VLCC lying at anchor. It needs no permit and no construction time, it can be hired for a few months and released again, and its capacity — 160,000 to 320,000 deadweight tonnes, of the order of two million barrels — is available immediately. Floating storage is therefore the top of the storage merit order: the most expensive unit, called only when everything cheaper is full.

The link to slide 282: in spring 2020 precisely this happened. Demand collapsed, onshore storage at Cushing filled, the forward curve went into deep contango and floating storage rose to record levels. Whoever could get neither a tank nor a ship had to pay someone else to take his physical barrel, which is why the expiring WTI contract settled below zero on 20 April 2020. The negative price was the price of storage scarcity, and the VLCC was the last available answer to it.

The side effect is that the same fleet is then not available for transport, so freight rates spike at the same moment: storage demand and transport demand compete for one asset.

prompt: The AFRA scale on the slide classifies tankers by deadweight. Name the classes with their size ranges and state which cargo each group carries. Why does the size ladder correlate with the cargo type?
solution:
The Average Freight Rate Assessment (AFRA) scale, in thousand deadweight metric tons (DWT):
- Refined products: GP (General Purpose) 10-25 DWT and MR (Medium Range) 25-45 DWT.
- Refined products or crude oil: LR1 (Long Range 1) 45-80 DWT, AFRA (AFRAMAX) 80-120 DWT and LR2 (Long Range 2) 80-160 DWT.
- Crude oil only: VLCC (Very Large Crude Carrier) 160-320 DWT and ULCC (Ultra Large Crude Carrier) 320-550 DWT.

Why the ladder correlates with the cargo: it is the same asymmetry as on slide 293. Crude moves in few very large intercontinental parcels from a handful of export regions, so the largest hulls with the lowest cost per tonne-mile are the right tool, and the buyer — a refinery — can absorb a parcel of two million barrels. Refined products move in many small parcels to many terminals, they come in several grades that must not be contaminated by each other, and the receiving ports are smaller and shallower. A product tanker therefore has to be small and to have segregated, coated tanks, while a crude carrier can be large and simple.

The binding limits at the top of the ladder are physical, not economic: draught and channel width. A VLCC cannot enter most product ports, and a fully laden ULCC cannot transit the Suez Canal, which is why the very largest ships serve only a few deepwater terminals and offshore loading buoys — and why the freight rate for the largest classes is set by a small number of routes.
